The National Institutes of Health (NIH) has spent the past decade compiling information on hundreds of U.S.-based scientists it believes tried to illegally help their country of origin, most often China. Dao remains an important player in the debate over research security. Now head of campus safety and research security at Rice University, he will be tackling a question that arguably should have been asked before NIH plunged ahead: How often do foreign governments try to steal research at U.S. universities?

article.plain_text:
NIH researchers examined how a person’s previous exposure to one dengue virus affects the body’s response to a second dengue infection. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease with four major virus types. A subsequent infection with a different virus type from the first infection can sometimes increase an individual’s risk of severe illness.
In a clinical trial with 45 healthy adults, researchers found that some existing immune responses may allow the virus to multiply more, while others can help the body control the virus. Each participant received a single injection of a live but weakened DENV3 virus, and researchers collected blood samples over time to measure the amount of virus in the blood, antibodies, T-cell responses, inflammatory proteins, and clinical symptoms. Statistical models determined which immune responses present before the challenge predicted viral replication and sustained immunity. A major finding was that prior immunity did not always provide the same protection. In fact, participants with certain preexisting antibodies experienced greater viral replication, while others with strong neutralizing antibodies and protective T-cell responses had very little viral replication.
The study identified immune markers that may help distinguish protection from increased risk. These findings could help researchers design vaccines that provide broad, long-lasting protection against all four types of dengue virus and develop better ways to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of future dengue vaccines and treatments.
Reference: Odio CD, Aogo RA, Firdous S, et al. Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses. Science Translational Medicine. DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed.aei511
